tagline: Eleven miles beside the Mad River, with limestone cliffs and wetlands.
intro: Lower Valley Pike follows County Road 316 for 11 miles. The Mad River runs beside the byway, with limestone cliffs, riverside woods and wetlands along the corridor. Ohio’s byways brochure highlights canoeing, fishing and wildlife observation on the river.

At Piqua on the Mad River in 1780, George Rogers Clark’s Kentucky militia fought Shawnee people under Chief Black Hoof. The militia drove the Shawnee from the village and burned it and the surrounding fields.
Begin with Medway, named for its position midway between Springfield and Dayton. Continue toward Limestone City, whose name records the local limestone-quarrying industry.

moments.title: Medway
moments.text: Medway’s name describes a relationship between towns: the community was named for its midway position between Springfield and Dayton. It was platted in 1816, and a post office named Medway has operated since 1850.

moments.title: Peckuwe
moments.text: The battle at Piqua on August 8, 1780, brought George Rogers Clark’s Kentucky militia against Shawnee people led by Chief Black Hoof. Clark’s artillery bombarded the stockade from cliffs above the village. His men then spent two days burning as much as 500 acres of corn. The Shawnee moved to the Great Miami River instead of rebuilding here, naming their new village Peckuwe. Their new settlement lay just north of the modern town of Piqua, Ohio. The Clark County Historical Society later built a memorial trail and park on the battlefield.

moments.title: Limestone City
moments.text: Limestone City was platted in 1886 and named for the local limestone-quarrying industry. It is an unincorporated community in Clark County.
